results.title: The distance decay effect and spatial reach of spillovers | Journal of Geographical Systems | Springer Nature Link
results.content: # The distance decay effect and spatial reach of spillovers. This paper quantifies and graphically illustrates the distance decay effect and spatial reach of spillover effects derived from a spatial Durbin (SD) model with parameterized spatial weight matrices. Building on attributes of the concept of spatial autocorrelation developed by Arthur Getis, we adopt a distance-based negative exponential spatial weight matrix and parameterize it by a decay parameter that is different for each spatial lag in this model, both of the regressand and of all regressors. The quantification and illustration are applied to the spatially augmented neoclassical growth framework, which we estimate using data for 266 NUTS-2 regions in the EU over the period 2000–2018. We find distance decay parameters ranging from 0.233 to 2.224 and spatial reaches ranging from 700 to more than 1500 km for the different growth determinants in this model. These wide ranges highlight the restrictiveness of the conventional SD model based on one common spatial weight matrix for all spatial lags.

results.content: Surrounded by wars: Quantifying the role of spatial conflict spillovers - ScienceDirect Skip to main contentSkip to article Volume 49, March 2016, Pages 7-16 Surrounded by wars: Quantifying the role of spatial conflict spillovers Author links open overlay panelFabrizio Carmignani, Parvinder Kler We apply panel estimation methods to test how the incidence of war in neighbourhood countries affects the incidence of war in the domestic country. This study finds positive and significant evidence of “spatial conflict spillover”: higher incidence in the neighbourhood increases domestic country involvement in war. From direct military action crossing over to neighbouring countries to indirect negative impacts on their budgetary and fiscal positions due to having to care for refugees leaving conflict zones, the spillover costs of neighbourhood wars on an otherwise peaceful country can be significant. Yet the voluminous research dedicated to studying the determinants of wars and/or its impact on national incomes has largely been unable to test for the outcome of conflict spillover. Specifically, in this paper we study how the incidence of war (civil and interstate) in neighbourhood countries affects the incidence of war in the domestic country. Firstly, we find that neighbourhood wars are significant predictors of spatial conflict spillovers, even after controlling for a number of geographic, economic, and institutional characteristics of the home country. results.content:
Title: Difference-in-Differences Estimation with Spatial Spillovers - ADS
## ADS. ## Difference-in-Differences Estimation with Spatial Spillovers. #### Abstract. Empirical work often uses treatment assigned following geographic boundaries. When the effects of treatment cross over borders, classical difference-in-differences estimation produces biased estimates for the average treatment effect. In this paper, I introduce a potential outcomes framework to model spillover effects and decompose the estimate's bias in two parts: (1) the control group no longer identifies the counterfactual trend because their outcomes are affected by treatment and (2) changes in treated units' outcomes reflect the effect of their own treatment status and the effect from the treatment status of 'close' units. I propose conditions for non-parametric identification that can remove both sources of bias and semi-parametrically estimate the spillover effects themselves including in settings with staggered treatment timing. To highlight the importance of spillover effects, I revisit analyses of three place-based interventions. :   10.48550/arXiv.2105.03737. :   34 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables.

results.title: Spatial spillover: Significance and symbolism
results.content:
Title: Spatial spillover: Significance and symbolism
# Significance of Spatial spillover. Spatial spillover refers to the impact of activities or policies in one region on surrounding regions. Research indicates that these spillovers can have both positive and negative effects. Infrastructure differences influence the spatial spillover of energy consumption among cities. Further research could consider the spatial spillover of environmental effects caused by environmental decentralization due to local competition. ## The concept of Spatial spillover in scientific sources. Spatial spillover refers to the impact of activities/policies in one region on surrounding regions. It affects China's carbon intensity, energy consumption, environmental regulation, and decentralization, with both positive and negative economic and environmental effects. (1) Spatial spillover refers to the geographical spread of influence, which Liu and colleagues investigated using seven socioeconomic drivers to check their impacts on haze pollution levels. (2) Spatial spillover describes the mechanism through which the employment effects stemming from China’s carbon emission trading policy are observed to propagate or influence geographically distinct areas. (3) Spatial spillovers refer to the indirect effects of economic activities that spread across geographical areas, a concept used when examining the digital economy's impact on forestry green total factor productivity. (4) The phenomenon where the effects of an action, such as the development of new technology, extend beyond the immediate location to influence surrounding or related geographical areas. (5) An effect originating from a policy implementation in one area that subsequently spreads its influence, in this case, a positive impact on business creation in neighboring territories. (1) Spatial Spillover refers to effects that are studied in relation to environmental regulations impacting haze pollution, suggesting a geographical diffusion of regulatory consequences across regions. (2) This concept describes how economic growth in one geographical area can have an effect, positive or negative, on the economic performance of neighboring or related regions within the country. (3) Spatial spillover is an effect that must be accounted for when assessing the impact of technological innovation and industrial structure upgrades on ecological efficiency in China. (4) Spatial spillovers, along with threshold effects, of internet development and entrepreneurship on green innovation efficiency in China are investigated in reference number forty-nine, revealing geographical influence.
